body.en: There are two ways to version a database: **migration-based** (a sequence of change scripts — EF Core migrations, Flyway) and **state-based / declarative** (files describe the desired END STATE; a tool computes the change script). SQL Database Projects are declarative: each object is defined ONCE in a `.sql` file with `CREATE` syntax; to change a table you edit its CREATE TABLE file, and the deployment engine (DacFx) works out the `ALTER`. As a .NET developer, think of it as 'csproj for databases'.

The modern format uses the **Microsoft.Build.Sql** MSBuild SDK — the format used by the VS Code SQL Database Projects extension and by SQL database in Fabric source control; recommended for new work. Benefits over original (.NET Framework) projects: cross-platform builds on .NET 8+ (`dotnet build`), **NuGet package references** for database references (e.g. system databases), and **default globbing** — all `.sql` files in the folder are included automatically, so the project file doesn't list every object (far fewer merge conflicts). Create with the `Microsoft.Build.Sql.Templates` package: `dotnet new sqlproj`. Original projects can be converted by editing the project file; SQLCLR still needs .NET Framework to build.

sections.code:
<!-- AdventureWorks.sqlproj (SDK-style) -->
<Project Sdk="Microsoft.Build.Sql/1.0.0">
  <PropertyGroup>
    <Name>AdventureWorks</Name>
    <DSP>Microsoft.Data.Tools.Schema.Sql.SqlAzureV12DatabaseSchemaProvider</DSP>
    <RunSqlCodeAnalysis>true</RunSqlCodeAnalysis>
  </PropertyGroup>
  <ItemGroup>
    <!-- system database reference; pick the package version matching your target platform -->
    <PackageReference Include="Microsoft.SqlServer.Dacpacs.Master" Version="x.y.z" />
  </ItemGroup>
</Project>

body.en:
`dotnet build` compiles the model and validates it:
- **Reference validation**: a view referencing a missing table/column fails the build (unresolved reference errors like SQL71501).
- **Target platform** (DSP property): syntax and features are validated against a specific SQL version — e.g. JSON functions from SQL Server 2022 fail on a Sql140 target; choose Azure SQL Database, SQL Server 2025, Fabric SQL database etc.
- **Code analysis** (optional, `RunSqlCodeAnalysis`): best-practice rules (SR0001 'avoid SELECT *', etc.) reported as warnings or configurable errors.
The output artifact is a **.dacpac** (data-tier application package) in bin/Debug or bin/Release — a portable, versionable model of the schema. Builds don't need a live database, so they run anywhere, including CI agents.

sections.code:
dotnet new install Microsoft.Build.Sql.Templates
dotnet new sqlproj -n AdventureWorks
dotnet build AdventureWorks/AdventureWorks.sqlproj -c Release
# -> bin/Release/AdventureWorks.dacpac

body.en:
Objects often reference things outside the project:
- **System databases** (master/msdb): add package references (e.g. `Microsoft.SqlServer.Dacpacs.Master`) so references to sys objects resolve.
- **Other projects or .dacpacs, same database**: split a large schema into multiple projects composed into one database.
- **Different database, same server / different server**: references use SQLCMD variables for database (and server) names, e.g. `[$(SalesDb)].dbo.Orders`, so names can differ per environment.
Unresolved external references become build warnings/errors — references are how you make validation complete.

Each project can have ONE pre-deployment and ONE post-deployment script (they can include other files with SQLCMD `:r`). Pre-deployment runs before the schema changes (e.g. data fix-ups needed for a change); post-deployment runs after (e.g. seeding). **Reference/static data** (country codes, order statuses, feature flags) belongs in source control too: write **idempotent** post-deployment scripts — typically `MERGE` from a VALUES list — so every deployment converges the table to the expected rows without duplicates. Keep scripts re-runnable; deployments run them every time.

sections.code:
-- Script.PostDeployment.sql
MERGE dbo.OrderStatus AS tgt
USING (VALUES (1, N'New'), (2, N'Shipped'), (3, N'Cancelled')) AS src (StatusId, Name)
    ON tgt.StatusId = src.StatusId
WHEN MATCHED AND tgt.Name <> src.Name THEN UPDATE SET Name = src.Name
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY TARGET THEN INSERT (StatusId, Name) VALUES (src.StatusId, src.Name)
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE THEN DELETE;

body.en:
Deploy the .dacpac with **SqlPackage** (cross-platform CLI) — actions you should know:
- `/Action:Publish` — compare dacpac to target and apply changes (new or existing databases; one dacpac can upgrade a fleet).
- `/Action:Script` — generate the T-SQL deployment script without running it (for review).
- `/Action:DeployReport` — XML report of the changes a publish would make.
- `/Action:DriftReport` — changes made to a registered database since its last deployment (schema drift).
- `/Action:Extract` — create a .dacpac from an existing database (start a project from production).
**Publish profiles** (`*.publish.xml`) store deployment options per environment: `BlockOnPossibleDataLoss` (default true — stops deployments that would lose data), `DropObjectsNotInSource`, SQLCMD variable values, etc.

examTips.en: SDK-style = Microsoft.Build.Sql, dotnet build, cross-platform, NuGet package references, default .sql globbing (fewer project-file merge conflicts).
Build validates references and target-platform syntax and outputs a .dacpac — no live database needed.
Target platform (DSP) mismatch is a classic build-failure cause for new syntax (JSON, vector, REGEXP).
One pre- and one post-deployment script per project; use :r to include more; scripts must be idempotent.
Reference/static data → MERGE in post-deployment script, stored in source control.
SqlPackage actions: Publish, Script, DeployReport, DriftReport, Extract. BlockOnPossibleDataLoss defaults to true.
Cross-database references use SQLCMD variables so database names can vary by environment.
